newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pharmacia & Upjohn warns about earnings.
newsitem.headline: Pharmacia & Upjohn warns about earnings.

text.p: Troubled U.S.-Swedish drug company Pharmacia & Upjohn said Thursday its second-quarter earnings would be lower than the first quarter's and that negative sales and profit trends would continue through the rest of the year.

The announcement was tantamount to the fourth profit warning in nine months from P&U, which has been beset with problems since it was formed in 1995 through the merger of Kalamazoo, Mich.-based Upjohn and Sweden's Pharmacia.

"Everyone knew they had a difficult quarter and that sales and profit were under pressure," said analyst James McKean from Morgan Stanley. "The main thing now is to stop the declining sales in the existing portfolio and boost its new products."
Analysts said a major problem faced by the company was that its portfolio consisted mainly of mature products and it needed to focus more on key products.
"They have a strong pipeline but these products need to be launched and need time to grow before compensating for the other products," said Ohman analyst Gustav Lenman.
The company also needs to resolve its generic problems in the United States, but this would probably take more time, analysts said.

P&U's new chief executive, Fred Hassan, appointed just last month, said the company planned various measures to reverse the negative trends, including simplifying the company's structure and decision-making systems whle concentrating investment on research and development.
"Although they are initially concentrated on growth, we expect they will also give important cost savings which will be quantified later this year," Hassan said in a statement.
"We expect to receive benefits beginning in 1998 from the actions now being taken."
The moves by Hassan, successor to John Zabriskie, who left the company suddenly in January, were welcomed by analysts.
"I think it looks quite good. Despite the veiled profit warning, it seems the new CEO is doing all the right things that should have been done long ago," said Merrill Lynch analyst Janet Dyson.

The dismantling of the group's three pharmaceutical product centres in Europe and the United States was seen as particularly positive, increasing accountability to Hassan and stopping duplication of costs.
Sales, marketing and Phase IV clinical research will come under one single worldwide umbrella while research and development will now come under one executive, Goran Ando.
The restructuring programme was seen as step in the right direction, although the benefits would not hit the bottom line until 1998, and maybe not till the second half.
"The structure has needed to be cleared up," said McKean.
"What they need now is to get a couple of good quarters behind them to get some confidence back in the stock."
